sources.text: Where an area under consideration contains multiple functions having different occupant load factors, the design occupant load for such area shall be based on the floor area of each function calculated independently.

For areas without fixed seating, the occupant load shall be not less than that number determined by dividing the floor area under consideration by the occupant load factor assigned to the function of the space as set forth in Table 1004.1.3.

Where the actual number of occupants of any space will be significantly lower than listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the commissioner may establish a lower basis for the determination of the number of occupants.

For areas having fixed seats and aisles, the occupant load shall be determined by the number of fixed seats installed therein. The occupant load for areas in which fixed seating is not installed, such as waiting spaces, shall be determined in accordance with Section 1004.1.3 and added to the number of fixed seats.

1004.1 1004.1 Design occupant load. Design occupant load. In determining means of egress requirements, the number of occupants for whom means of egress facilities shall be provided shall be established by the largest number computed in accordance with Section 1004.1.3, unless otherwise permitted by Section 1004.1.3.1, 1004.1.3.2 or 1004.2.

1004.1.3.2 1004.1.3.2 Unlisted functions. Where data regarding the square feet area per person for a function is not listed in Table 1004.1.3 , the occupant load shall be established by a registered design professional, subject to the approval of the commissioner.

1004.1.1.2.3 1004.1.1.2.3 Group R-2 accessory spaces as primary function on a story. Where the aggregate Group R-2 occupancy accessory area of all rooms, areas or spaces, including outdoor spaces that are not provided with independent means of egress and that do not converge into interior means of egress, exceed 50 percent of the building area of the story in which they are located, and the total number of occupants on such story exceeds 150 persons, the following conditions shall apply: 1. The interior corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be constructed as public corridors in accordance with Table 1020.1.2 with 1-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers, and 2-hour fire-resistance-rated fire barriers where a dead-end corridor exceeds 40 feet (12 192 mm) in length; 2. Access to the corridors shall be limited to those necessary for exit access through the corridor from normally occupied spaces. Direct openings from the mechanical, electrical and other storage spaces shall not be permitted, except that access to the corridor may be provided through a vestibule constructed with fire barriers, with a minimum fire-resistance rating consistent with the required hourly rating for the corridor; 3. Corridors or portions thereof serving such accessory spaces shall be sufficient to accommodate a total occupant load on the basis of 3 square feet (0.28 m 2 ) per person; 4. The minimum dimension of such corridors shall be sufficient to accommodate the total occupant load discharging into such corridors, but shall in no case be less than 5 feet (1524 mm) in minimum dimension; and 5. In addition to Conditions 1 through 4 above, one of the following conditions shall be met: 5.1. Each of the interior exit stairways and ramps serving such story shall be protected by a smokeproof enclosure in accordance with Section 909.20; 5.2. The corridor or portions of the corridor serving the rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall be pressurized in accordance with requirements that are applicable to interior exit stairways. Connecting interior exit stairways need not be pressurized unless otherwise required by this code; 5.3. All passenger elevators serving the rooms, areas, or spaces that are accessory to the Group R-2 occupancy shall comply with occupant self-evacuation elevator requirements in Section 3008.1 through 3008.11; or 5.4. One additional exit stairway meeting the requirements of Sections 1009 and 1023 shall be provided in addition to the minimum number of exits required by Section 1006 . The total width of any combination of remaining exit stairways with one exit stairway removed shall not be less than the total width required by Section 1005.3. Rooms, areas or spaces that do not comply with the conditions in Sections 1004.1.1.2.1 and 1004.1.1.2.2, or Section 1004.1.1.2.3 where applicable, shall have occupant loads calculated cumulatively per story and be classified as Occupancy Group A.

1004.1.1.2 1004.1.1.2 Cumulative occupant loads in Group R-2 occupancies. Rooms, areas or spaces that are accessory to a Group R-2 occupancy and that comply with the conditions below may have occupant loads calculated individually per room, area, or space, and be classified as Occupancy Group R-2.

CERTIFICATE OF OPERATION. A certificate issued by the department upon satisfactory inspection of a specific piece of hoisting equipment to ensure that the equipment is in compliance with this code. DWELLING UNIT. A single unit consisting of one or more habitable rooms and occupied or arranged to be occupied as a unit separate from all other units within a dwelling. EXIT ACCESS. That portion of a means of egress system that leads from any occupied portion of a building or structure to an exit. FIXED SEATING. Furniture or fixture designed and installed for the use of sitting and secured in place including bench-type seats and seats with or without backs or arm rests. INTERIOR EXIT STAIRWAY. An exit component that serves to meet one or more means of egress design requirements, such as required number of exits or exit access travel distance, and provides for a protected path of egress travel to the exit discharge or public way. OCCUPANT LOAD . The number of persons for which the means of egress of a building or portion thereof is designed . PARKING GARAGE. A structure or portion of a structure, other than a private garage or carport, used for the parking or storage of motor vehicles. WHEELCHAIR SPACE . A space for a single wheelchair and its occupant .
402.8.2 402.8.2 Occupant load. The calculated occupant load used to determine the required number of means of egress shall be in accordance with this section.

303.7 303.7 Certificate of Operation. A Certificate of Operation shall be required, as per Section 28-117.1 , for the following assembly occupancies: 1. Indoor assembly occupancies used or intended for use by 75 persons or more, including open spaces at 20 feet (6096 mm) or more above or below grade plane, such as roofs or roof terraces. 2. Outdoor assembly occupancies used and intended for use by 200 persons or more. Section BC 304: Business Group B

1108.2.3 1108.2.3 Companion seats. At least one companion seat complying with ICC A117.1, including Section 802.7 (Companion Seat), shall be provided for each wheelchair space required by Sections 1108.2.2.1 through 1108.2.2.3 of this code.

issues.detail: The answer states that conference, soft-seating, and coffee-break/lounge functions “cannot simply be omitted” based on the nonsimultaneous-use premise and that the provisions “require function-by-function area calculations.” BC 1004.1.2 requires independent calculations when multiple functions have different occupant-load factors, but the supplied evidence does not establish whether nonsimultaneous functions may be omitted or otherwise treated under the code. The supported conclusion should be that the proposed nonsimultaneous treatment is not established by the supplied evidence, not that the code affirmatively prohibits omitting those functions.

exactPassages: Additions, alterations, renovations or repairs to existing systems shall conform to that required for new systems without requiring the existing system to comply with all of the requirements of this code, except as otherwise required in Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6. Additions, alterations or repairs shall not cause an existing installation to become unsafe, hazardous or overloaded.
Fire protection systems governed by this chapter shall be provided:
1. To the entire building as if the building were hereafter erected, where a change is made in the main use or dominant occupancy of such building.
2. Throughout a space, where a change is made in the occupancy group classification or usage of the space.
selectedEvidence.resolvedTitle: 901.9.2 Additional requirements based on change of occupancy or use.

exactPassages: Fire protection systems shall be provided in enlarged portions of a building and where this chapter would require such systems in new construction for a space or building.

Group B occupancies having a total gross area exceeding 100,000 square feet (9290.3 m 2 ) located in buildings where the highest occupied floor is 75 feet (22 860 mm) or less above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access shall be provided with automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire alarm system in accordance with Section 907.2.13.1 and an emergency voice/alarm communication system in accordance with Section 907.5.2.2 that initiates a total evacuation signal.

testCase.question: An existing prior-code Group B building has a previously approved legacy fire-alarm system. A proposed enlargement does not change the stated use or occupancy, but the resulting Group B gross area may exceed 100,000 square feet. The height of the highest occupied floor above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access has not been confirmed. Does the selected 2022 Building Code evidence automatically require replacement of the entire legacy system, and what additional facts determine the required scope?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The enlargement does not, by itself, prove that the entire legacy system must be replaced. BC 901.9.1 requires additions and alterations to existing systems to comply with new-system requirements without automatically requiring the entire existing system to comply, subject to the additional triggers in Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6. BC 901.9.3 requires fire-protection systems in enlarged portions and where Chapter 9 would require them for new construction. If the resulting Group B occupancy exceeds 100,000 square feet and the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level, BC 907.2.2.2 requires the identified smoke-detection, fire-alarm, and emergency voice/alarm systems for the qualifying Group B occupancy; that requirement cannot automatically be limited to only the enlarged portion. On the stated facts, BC 901.9.2 is not triggered unless the asserted absence of an occupancy or use change is incorrect. A main-use or dominant-occupancy change applies to the entire building; a space occupancy-classification or usage change applies throughout that space. The selected evidence does not determine whether the legacy equipment can be extended, interfaced, or retained, or whether technical conditions ultimately require modification or replacement. Applicable Buildings Bulletin 2024-001 conditions and project-specific DOB and FDNY review remain necessary outside the selected evidence.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected passages establish upgrade triggers and scope principles, but they cannot establish whether the existing system may be retained or must be replaced without project-specific system, occupancy, area, height, and compatibility facts.

answer.answerText:
No. On the stated facts, the selected provisions do not automatically require replacement of the entire previously approved legacy fire-alarm system merely because the building is enlarged or may exceed 100,000 square feet. Work on the existing system must meet the requirements for new systems, but BC 901.9.1 expressly does not require the existing system as a whole to comply with every current-code requirement. The alteration also may not make the installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

The enlargement itself must receive fire-protection systems where required for new construction. If the resulting Group B occupancy has total gross area exceeding 100,000 square feet **and** the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access, BC 907.2.2.2 requires automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire-alarm system and an emergency voice/alarm communication system that initiates a total-evacuation signal. That provision establishes required functions; the selected text does not say that compliance necessarily requires wholesale replacement rather than a code-compliant addition, alteration, or integration of the approved system.

There is no stated main-use/dominant-occupancy change or space occupancy/usage change. Therefore, the selected change-of-use provisions do not presently trigger their respective whole-building or throughout-the-space requirements. If either change occurs, the main-use/dominant-occupancy rule requires Chapter 9 systems throughout the building as though newly erected; a change in a space's occupancy-group classification or usage requires them throughout that space.

The material facts still needed to determine scope are: (1) the actual total gross area after the work—whether it exceeds, not merely may exceed, 100,000 square feet; (2) the height of the highest occupied floor above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level, including whether it is 75 feet or less; (3) the precise enlargement and fire-alarm modification design; (4) existing-system capacity and compatibility to serve any required detection and voice/alarm functions without becoming overloaded; (5) whether any main use, dominant occupancy, occupancy classification, or usage changes; and (6) whether another applicable Chapter 9 trigger applies. In addition, the selected evidence does not establish whether the enlargement increases the prior-code building's floor surface area by more than 110 percent; if it does, AC 28-101.4.5 states that the entire building must comply as a new building, which could change the result substantially.
answer.conclusion: No. On the stated facts, the selected provisions do not automatically require replacement of the entire previously approved legacy fire-alarm system merely because the building is enlarged or may exceed 100,000 square feet. Work on the existing system must meet the requirements for new systems, but BC 901.9.1 expressly does not require the existing system as a whole to comply with every current-code requirement. The alteration also may not make the installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

supportedPoints.heading: Existing-system work is not automatically a whole-system upgrade
supportedPoints.explanation: Additions, alterations, renovations, and repairs to an existing fire-protection system must conform to new-system requirements, but the existing system is not thereby required to comply with all current-code requirements. The work cannot make the installation unsafe, hazardous, or overloaded.

supportedPoints.heading: An enlargement requires new-construction fire-protection systems where applicable
supportedPoints.explanation: Fire-protection systems must be provided in enlarged portions and wherever Chapter 9 would require them for new construction for the relevant space or building.

supportedPoints.heading: Large Group B buildings have a conditional alarm and voice requirement
supportedPoints.explanation: For a Group B occupancy with total gross area exceeding 100,000 square feet, the requirement applies only where the highest occupied floor is 75 feet or less above the lowest Fire Department vehicle-access level. It requires automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire-alarm system and an emergency voice/alarm communication system initiating a total-evacuation signal.

supportedPoints.heading: Use or occupancy changes can expand the required scope
supportedPoints.explanation: Chapter 9 fire-protection systems must be provided throughout the building as though newly erected if the main use or dominant occupancy changes. They must be provided throughout a space if that space's occupancy-group classification or usage changes.

citations.title: § 28-101.4.5 Work that increases existing floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110 percent.

supportingPassages.selectedText: 28-101.4.5 § 28-101.4.5 Work that increases existing floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110 percent. Notwithstanding sections 28-101.4.3 and 28-102.4.3 or any other provision of this code that would authorize alterations of prior code buildings in accordance with the 1968 building code or prior codes, where the proposed work at the completion of construction will increase the amount of floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110%, over the amount of existing floor surface area, such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if it were a new building hereafter erected. See section 28-105.2 for permits for such work. Exceptions. When determining the amount of existing floor surface area for the purposes of section 28-101.4.5 , the following shall be excluded from the measured square footage of floor surface area: 1. The square footage of floors removed during the course of the work when such floors are removed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade. 2. The square footage of any floor that was installed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade less than 12 months prior to submission of the application for construction document approval for the proposed work. For the purposes of this exception, floors installed pursuant to a work permit signed off less than 12 months before such submission shall not be counted as existing floor surface area.

citations.relevance: Establishes the separate prior-code-building consequence if floor surface area increases by more than 110 percent.

sources.text: Additions, alterations, renovations or repairs to existing systems shall conform to that required for new systems without requiring the existing system to comply with all of the requirements of this code, except as otherwise required in Sections 901.9.2 through 901.9.6. Additions, alterations or repairs shall not cause an existing installation to become unsafe, hazardous or overloaded.
Fire protection systems governed by this chapter shall be provided:
1. To the entire building as if the building were hereafter erected, where a change is made in the main use or dominant occupancy of such building.
2. Throughout a space, where a change is made in the occupancy group classification or usage of the space.
Fire protection systems shall be provided in enlarged portions of a building and where this chapter would require such systems in new construction for a space or building.

Group B occupancies having a total gross area exceeding 100,000 square feet (9290.3 m 2 ) located in buildings where the highest occupied floor is 75 feet (22 860 mm) or less above the lowest level of Fire Department vehicle access shall be provided with automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire alarm system in accordance with Section 907.2.13.1 and an emergency voice/alarm communication system in accordance with Section 907.5.2.2 that initiates a total evacuation signal.

AREA, BUILDING. The area included within surrounding exterior walls (or exterior walls and firewalls) exclusive of vent shafts and courts. Areas of the building not provided with surrounding walls shall be included in the building area if such areas are included within the horizontal projection of the roof or floor above. CONSTRUCTION. The excavation, erection, alteration, and repair of buildings or any component parts, including all operations incidental thereto. DWELLING. A building or structure that is occupied in whole or in part as the home, residence or sleeping place of one or more families. EMERGENCY VOICE/ALARM COMMUNICATIONS. Dedicated manual or automatic facilities for originating and distributing voice instructions, as well as alert and evacuation signals pertaining to a fire or other emergency, to the occupants of a building. FIRE ALARM SYSTEM . A system or portion of a combination system consisting of components and circuits arranged to monitor and annunciate the status of fire alarm or supervisory signal - initiating devices and to initiate the appropriate response to those signals . FIRE PROTECTION SYSTEM. Approved devices, equipment and systems or combinations of systems used to detect a fire, activate an alarm, extinguish or control a fire, control or manage smoke and products of a fire or any combination thereof. NEW CONSTRUCTION. See Section G201.1.2. SMOKE. Air-borne solid and liquid particulates and gases evolved when a material undergoes pyrolysis or combustion, including the quality of air that is entrained or otherwise mixed into the mass.

28-101.4.5 § 28-101.4.5 Work that increases existing floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110 percent. Notwithstanding sections 28-101.4.3 and 28-102.4.3 or any other provision of this code that would authorize alterations of prior code buildings in accordance with the 1968 building code or prior codes, where the proposed work at the completion of construction will increase the amount of floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110%, over the amount of existing floor surface area, such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if it were a new building hereafter erected. See section 28-105.2 for permits for such work. Exceptions. When determining the amount of existing floor surface area for the purposes of section 28-101.4.5 , the following shall be excluded from the measured square footage of floor surface area: 1. The square footage of floors removed during the course of the work when such floors are removed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade. 2. The square footage of any floor that was installed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade less than 12 months prior to submission of the application for construction document approval for the proposed work. For the purposes of this exception, floors installed pursuant to a work permit signed off less than 12 months before such submission shall not be counted as existing floor surface area.

28-101.4.5.1 § 28-101.4.5.1 Changes in scope of work. In cases where changes in the scope of work during the course of construction would result in increasing the floor surface area at the completion of construction by more than 110 percent, over the amount of existing floor surface area as determined pursuant to section 28-101.4.5 , such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if hereafter erected and such work shall be refiled as a new building application in accordance with the provisions of section 28-105.2 . Exception: Work to the extent necessary to relieve an emergency condition may be performed prior to amending plans or obtaining a new permit pursuant to sections 28-105.4.1 and 28-105.12.2 .

28-101.4.5.2 § 28-101.4.5.2 Definitions. As used in Section 28-101.4.5 , the following term shall have the following meaning unless the context or subject matter requires otherwise. FLOOR SURFACE AREA. Floor surface area is the gross square foot area of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces, including roofs of bulkheads and superstructures, of a building or structure at any level, including cellar, attic and roof.
29-101 Short title. This title shall be known as and may be cited as the "New York city fire code" or the "fire code."

Any applicable seismic loads and requirements shall be permitted to be determined in accordance with Chapter 16 of this code or the 1968 Building Code and Reference Standard RS 9-6 of such code. 901.9.4 901.9.4 Additional requirements based on value of alterations. Fire protection systems shall be provided to buildings and spaces in accordance with the provisions of Sections 901.9.4.1 through 901.9.4.3.

citationSupport.rationale: Each cited provision supports the proposition attributed to it. BC 901.9.1 supports the baseline new-work rule and no automatic whole-system compliance; BC 901.9.3 supports the enlargement/new-construction trigger; BC 907.2.2.2 supports both stated Group B conditions and listed systems; BC 901.9.2 supports the building-wide versus space-wide consequences of the specified changes. AC 28-101.4.5 is also accurately characterized as a separate, conditional issue.

unsupportedInventedClaims.rationale: The answer does not invent a requirement that the legacy system can remain, be integrated, or be replaced. It appropriately frames integration as unresolved and conditional. Its discussion of the 110-percent prior-code-building provision is supported by supplied enacted evidence.

appropriateUncertainty.rationale: The response conditions the Group B alarm requirement on both area and height, states that the area only may exceed the threshold, and explains that selected text cannot resolve retention, integration, or replacement of the legacy system.

evidenceInsufficiencyRecognition.rationale: The answer directly states that the supplied evidence does not prescribe the technical method of integrating, modifying, or replacing the legacy system and does not include other potentially applicable Chapter 9 triggers.

practicalUsefulness.rationale: It gives a clear no-automatic-replacement conclusion, applies the conditional triggers, identifies concrete needed facts, and requests drawings, system records, height data, and area calculations needed for follow-on analysis.

directlyAddressesQuestion.rationale: The response directly answers whether entire-system replacement is automatic and then identifies the facts governing scope.

requiredConcepts.rationale: It expressly rejects automatic whole-system replacement based solely on enlargement or possible area growth.

It accurately explains that work on an existing system must meet new-system requirements but that BC 901.9.1 does not automatically require the entire existing system to meet every current requirement.
It explains that enlarged portions require fire-protection systems where those systems would be required in new construction.
It distinguishes a main-use/dominant-occupancy change, which invokes building-wide treatment, from a space classification or usage change, which applies throughout that space.
It applies both BC 907.2.2.2 conditions: total gross Group B area exceeding 100,000 square feet and highest occupied floor no more than 75 feet above the specified vehicle-access level.
It identifies automatic smoke detection connected to an automatic fire-alarm system and an emergency voice/alarm communication system initiating a total-evacuation signal.

It frames BC 907.2.2.2 as applying where the resulting Group B occupancy meets both conditions and does not state that the requirement is confined to the enlargement. It further says the provision's compliance method remains unresolved rather than treating the required systems as enlargement-only work.
It expressly says that the selected text does not establish whether compliance entails integration, modification, or wholesale replacement of the legacy system.

It requests material project and existing-system information, including final area, height, enlargement/design scope, system capacity and compatibility, occupancy/use changes, Chapter 9 triggers, drawings, and approval records.

answer.answerText:
No. The selected Building Code passages do not address amendment of a Certificate of Occupancy or provide an exception from that requirement. They therefore cannot establish that a B-to-M change qualifies for such an exception. The applicable Administrative Code exception and any official guidance are not supplied.

The accessibility consequence that can be stated is conditional. If this is a prior-code building and the work is an alteration (rather than an ordinary repair), BC 1101.3 applies Chapter 11 to the alteration and to changes of use or occupancy. Further, where an alteration is considered either a Building Code change in occupancy classification or a zoning-use-group change, accessible features and construction governed by Chapter 11 must be provided throughout the space, including its immediate entrance(s). The stated B/M labels and the post-2024 zoning renumbering do not, on these passages alone, establish either predicate. The actual former and proposed Building Code classifications and zoning use groups must be determined under their respective authorities.

The selected text does not state an accessibility exception based on a Certificate-of-Occupancy amendment exception. Thus, even if another authority ultimately provides a CO exception, these passages alone do not show that it eliminates the stated accessibility obligation.

exactPassages: Sidewalk cafes provided beyond the building line shall comply with the requirements of this section, the New York City Zoning Resolution, the Commissioners of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and Department of Transportation, and with the projection limitations of Chapter 32 of this code.
No part of any awning, enclosure, fixture, equipment or removable platform of a sidewalk cafe shall be located:
2. So as to obstruct any exit from a building;

testCase.question: A restaurant proposes a sidewalk café with furniture near a building exit and cellar hatch. The owner says outdoor-dining authorization allows the exterior seats to be counted separately from the interior PACO and eliminates further accessibility review. The documents do not say whether the café is beyond the building line, enclosed, or separated from the interior seating by a Section 713 fire partition. What can be concluded from the selected Building Code passages, and what remains unresolved?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The proposal cannot be approved from the selected evidence. If it is a sidewalk café beyond the building line, BC 3111.1 requires compliance not only with Section 3111 but also with Chapter 32 and separate zoning and agency requirements; the selected evidence does not provide those outside rules. BC 3111.4 prohibits café components from obstructing a building exit or cellar hatch. Its cellar-entrance exception is not automatic: it requires a special application, an easily removable and prominently designated platform designed under Section 3111.5, and a cellar entrance or areaway that is not required egress. BC 3111.6 makes Chapter 11 applicable to the café and its access. BC 1108.2.9.1 requires accessible seating and standing spaces equal to at least 10 percent of the total, with not less than one accessible space at each type of dining surface; those spaces must be distributed and located on a level served by an accessible route. BC 3111.7 supplies only a conditional rule for an enclosed sidewalk café: unless a Section 713 fire partition separates it from inside seating, its seating is added to the inside seating solely to determine whether a PACO is required. These passages do not establish the approved interior capacity, the treatment of every open exterior seating arrangement, property-line or operational jurisdiction, DOT authorization, electrical permitting, or overall approval.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected passages establish several conditional Building Code constraints, but they do not establish overall approval, current agency jurisdiction, lawful seating capacity, or electrical and operational requirements.

answer.answerText:
No. The selected Building Code passages do not support the owner’s claim that outdoor-dining authorization permits furniture to obstruct a building exit or cellar hatch, allows exterior seating to be counted separately in every circumstance, or eliminates accessibility review.

No part of a sidewalk café’s awning, enclosure, fixture, equipment, or removable platform may obstruct a building exit or a cellar access hatch or areaway. The only supplied hatch-cover exception is conditional: upon special application, the commissioner may permit an easily removable, prominently designated platform designed under Section 3111.5 to cover a cellar entrance or areaway that is not used as a required means of egress. The stated facts do not establish those conditions or the necessary approval. Because the exit and hatch geometry and furniture layout are unknown, compliance with the no-obstruction rule cannot be determined.

Accessibility review is not eliminated. Sidewalk cafés and access to them must comply with Chapter 11. For dining surfaces, the supplied Chapter 11 provision requires accessible dining surfaces equal to at least 10 percent of the total seating and standing spaces, and at least one accessible dining surface of each type. Those accessible surfaces must be distributed throughout the facility and be on a level served by an accessible route. The selected text does not establish a separate exterior-only accessibility calculation; the seating counts, dining-surface types, accessible distribution, and route information are missing.

For the limited purpose of determining whether a place of assembly certificate of operation is required, enclosed sidewalk-café seating must be added to indoor seating unless the café is separated from the indoor seating by fire partitions complying with Section 713. Since enclosure status, seating counts, and the asserted fire-partition separation are unknown, the selected passages do not establish whether the exterior seating can be excluded from that certificate determination.

If the café is beyond the building line, it must also comply with the Zoning Resolution, the requirements of the Commissioners of the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection and Department of Transportation, and Chapter 32 projection limitations. The operative outdoor-dining authorization and its conditions were not supplied, so these passages do not establish its effect.
answer.conclusion: No. The selected Building Code passages do not support the owner’s claim that outdoor-dining authorization permits furniture to obstruct a building exit or cellar hatch, allows exterior seating to be counted separately in every circumstance, or eliminates accessibility review.

A limited exception permits a commissioner-approved, easily removable, prominently designated platform designed under Section 3111.5 to cover a cellar entrance or areaway that is not used as a required means of egress.

Separately, there must be at least one accessible dining surface of each type. Accessible dining surfaces must be distributed throughout the facility and located on a level accessed by an accessible route.

supportedPoints.explanation: For an enclosed sidewalk café, seating must be added to indoor seating to determine whether a place of assembly certificate of operation is required, unless the café is separated from the indoor seating by fire partitions complying with Section 713.

testCase.title: Intermittent enclosed-garage ventilation detector controls

projectContext.project: Enclosed parking garage with an intermittently operated mechanical ventilation system
projectContext.proposedControl: Operate the ventilation system from carbon monoxide detectors only, using a 35 ppm carbon monoxide set point
unknowns: whether any other control sequence is proposed

exactPassages: Where mechanical ventilation systems for enclosed parking garages operate intermittently, such operation shall be automatic by means of carbon monoxide detectors applied in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors.
Such detectors shall be installed in accordance with their manufacturers' instructions.
Such systems shall operate automatically upon detection of a concentration of carbon monoxide of 25 parts per million (ppm) or nitrogen dioxide of 500 parts per billion (ppb).

testCase.question: An enclosed parking garage will use intermittent mechanical ventilation. The proposed controls use carbon monoxide detectors only and start the system at 35 ppm carbon monoxide. Based only on the selected Mechanical Code provision, is that control sequence compliant, and what can and cannot be concluded?
testCase.expectedConclusion: The proposed control sequence does not match MC 404.1. For intermittent operation in an enclosed parking garage, automatic operation must use carbon monoxide detectors in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors. The system must operate automatically when carbon monoxide reaches 25 ppm or nitrogen dioxide reaches 500 ppb, so a carbon-monoxide-only sequence at 35 ppm omits the required nitrogen dioxide detection and exceeds the stated carbon monoxide trigger. The detectors must also be installed according to their manufacturers' instructions. The selected provision does not establish detector quantity or placement, the complete ventilation rate and capacity, or compliance of the rest of the mechanical design.

expectedUncertainty.description: The selected provision resolves the detector types and automatic-operation thresholds, but it does not establish the complete ventilation-system design or detector layout.

answer.answerText:
No. Based only on MC 404.1, the proposed sequence is not compliant as described. For intermittently operated mechanical ventilation in an enclosed parking garage, automatic operation must use carbon monoxide detectors in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors. Carbon monoxide detectors alone do not satisfy that requirement. In addition, the system must operate automatically at detection of 25 ppm carbon monoxide or 500 ppb nitrogen dioxide; a 35 ppm carbon monoxide set point is above the specified carbon monoxide trigger.

The supplied provision also requires detector installation in accordance with the manufacturers’ instructions. Because the manufacturer instructions, detector locations, coverage, and full mechanical-system design were not supplied, this review cannot determine compliance with that installation requirement or overall mechanical-system compliance. It also cannot determine whether some additional control sequence, not described in the proposed CO-only sequence, is included. Those uncertainties do not change the direct conclusion that the described CO-only, 35 ppm sequence does not meet the quoted MC 404.1 requirements.
answer.conclusion: No. Based only on MC 404.1, the proposed sequence is not compliant as described. For intermittently operated mechanical ventilation in an enclosed parking garage, automatic operation must use carbon monoxide detectors in conjunction with nitrogen dioxide detectors. Carbon monoxide detectors alone do not satisfy that requirement. In addition, the system must operate automatically at detection of 25 ppm carbon monoxide or 500 ppb nitrogen dioxide; a 35 ppm carbon monoxide set point is above the specified carbon monoxide trigger.

A carbon-monoxide-only control sequence does not satisfy this stated requirement.

supportedPoints.heading: The automatic-start thresholds are lower than proposed
supportedPoints.explanation: The system must operate automatically upon detection of 25 ppm carbon monoxide or 500 ppb nitrogen dioxide. A 35 ppm carbon monoxide set point does not meet the stated 25 ppm carbon-monoxide trigger.

supportedPoints.explanation: The detectors must be installed in accordance with their manufacturers’ instructions. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the proposed installation satisfies that requirement.

projectContext.originalScope: Proposed floor-surface-area increase stated as 105 percent

exactPassages: Notwithstanding sections 28-101.4.3 and 28-102.4.3 or any other provision of this code that would authorize alterations of prior code buildings in accordance with the 1968 building code or prior codes, where the proposed work at the completion of construction will increase the amount of floor surface area of a prior code building by more than 110%, over the amount of existing floor surface area, such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if it were a new building hereafter erected. See section 28-105.2 for permits for such work.
Exceptions. When determining the amount of existing floor surface area for the purposes of section 28-101.4.5 , the following shall be excluded from the measured square footage of floor surface area:
1. The square footage of floors removed during the course of the work when such floors are removed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade.

2. The square footage of any floor that was installed together with the supporting beams, joists, decking and slabs on grade less than 12 months prior to submission of the application for construction document approval for the proposed work. For the purposes of this exception, floors installed pursuant to a work permit signed off less than 12 months before such submission shall not be counted as existing floor surface area.

exactPassages: In cases where changes in the scope of work during the course of construction would result in increasing the floor surface area at the completion of construction by more than 110 percent, over the amount of existing floor surface area as determined pursuant to section 28-101.4.5 , such entire building shall be made to comply with the provisions of this code as if hereafter erected and such work shall be refiled as a new building application in accordance with the provisions of section 28-105.2 .
Exception: Work to the extent necessary to relieve an emergency condition may be performed prior to amending plans or obtaining a new permit pursuant to sections 28-105.4.1 and 28-105.12.2 .
As used in Section 28-101.4.5 , the following term shall have the following meaning unless the context or subject matter requires otherwise.

FLOOR SURFACE AREA. Floor surface area is the gross square foot area of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces, including roofs of bulkheads and superstructures, of a building or structure at any level, including cellar, attic and roof.

testCase.question: A prior-code building was filed as an alteration based on a 105 percent floor-surface-area increase, but scope changes during construction may raise the increase to 115 percent. Can the project remain an alteration, what happens if the threshold is crossed, and what must be included or excluded when checking the percentage?
testCase.expectedConclusion: If verified scope changes increase floor surface area at completion by more than 110 percent over existing floor surface area as determined under AC 28-101.4.5, AC 28-101.4.5.1 requires the entire building to comply as if newly erected and requires the work to be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2. The narrow emergency exception allows only work necessary to relieve an emergency condition before plans are amended or a new permit is obtained. AC 28-101.4.5.2 defines floor surface area as the gross area of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces at every level, expressly including bulkhead and superstructure roofs, cellar, attic, and roof. When measuring existing floor surface area, AC 28-101.4.5 excludes qualifying floors removed with their supporting construction and qualifying floors installed with their supporting construction less than 12 months before the filing. The stated 105 and 115 percent estimates are not enough without verified measurements, dates, removed-floor scope, and filing facts.

expectedUncertainty.description: The legal consequence is supported if the correctly measured increase is more than 110 percent, but the selected evidence does not verify the project measurements, exclusions, dates, or filing facts.

answer.answerText:
No—if the properly calculated increase at completion is **more than 110 percent**, the project cannot remain under the prior-code alteration treatment. A 105 percent increase is below that threshold; a 115 percent increase is above it. Where a scope change during construction produces that above-110-percent result, the entire building must comply with the current code as though newly erected, and the work must be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2. The rule applies notwithstanding other authority that otherwise permits prior-code alteration treatment.

The calculation compares the completion increase against existing floor surface area determined under AC 28-101.4.5. Floor surface area is the gross square footage of **all horizontal floor and roof surfaces** at every level, including cellar, attic, roof, and roofs of bulkheads and superstructures. In establishing the existing-area baseline, exclude: (1) floor area removed during the work only where the floors are removed together with their supporting beams, joists, decking, and slabs on grade; and (2) floor area installed with that supporting construction less than 12 months before submission of the construction-document application. A floor installed under a work permit signed off less than 12 months before that submission is likewise not existing floor surface area. Thus, the stated 115 percent figure resolves the outcome only if it reflects these required inclusions and exclusions.

If there is an emergency, the supplied exception permits only work necessary to relieve the emergency condition before plans are amended or a new permit is obtained. It does not alter the above-110-percent consequence or eliminate the new-building refiling requirement.
answer.conclusion: No—if the properly calculated increase at completion is **more than 110 percent**, the project cannot remain under the prior-code alteration treatment. A 105 percent increase is below that threshold; a 115 percent increase is above it. Where a scope change during construction produces that above-110-percent result, the entire building must comply with the current code as though newly erected, and the work must be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2. The rule applies notwithstanding other authority that otherwise permits prior-code alteration treatment.

supportedPoints.heading: More than 110 percent triggers new-building treatment
supportedPoints.explanation: When proposed work will increase a prior-code building’s floor surface area by more than 110 percent over the existing floor surface area, the entire building must comply with the code as though newly erected, notwithstanding provisions that otherwise allow prior-code alteration treatment.

supportedPoints.heading: A scope change above the threshold requires refiling
supportedPoints.explanation: If a construction-phase scope change will result in a completion increase of more than 110 percent over existing floor surface area determined under AC 28-101.4.5, the entire building must comply as though newly erected and the work must be refiled as a new-building application under AC 28-105.2.

supportedPoints.heading: Floor surface area covers all horizontal floor and roof surfaces
supportedPoints.explanation: For the threshold calculation, floor surface area is the gross square foot area of all horizontal floor and roof surfaces at every level, including cellar, attic, roof, and roofs of bulkheads and superstructures.

supportedPoints.heading: Specified areas are excluded from the existing-area baseline
supportedPoints.explanation: The existing floor-surface-area measurement excludes qualifying floors removed during the work together with their supporting beams, joists, decking, and slabs on grade. It also excludes qualifying floors installed with that supporting construction less than 12 months before submission of the construction-document application; floors installed under a permit signed off less than 12 months before that submission are not counted as existing floor surface area.

supportedPoints.heading: Emergency work has a limited timing exception
supportedPoints.explanation: Work necessary to relieve an emergency condition may proceed before plans are amended or a new permit is obtained under the cited permit provisions. The exception is limited to work necessary to relieve that emergency condition.
